Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 96, verse 1–2:

﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ ﴿created man from a clot﴾ ﴿Read﴾ [al-'Alaq: 3].

This is the first of the Qur'an to be revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), as is established from 'Aisha, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), which will come shortly.

The opening of the surah with the word "Read" (iqra') is a notice that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would be a reader, i.e., one who recites a book after he had not recited a book before. He, exalted is He, said: (﴿You did not recite any book before it﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48]), meaning before the revelation of the Qur'an. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Gabriel when he said to him "Read": "I am not a reader."
In this opening there is an excellent introduction (bara'at istihlal) to the Qur'an.

His saying, exalted is He: "Read" (iqra') is a command to recitation, and recitation (qira'ah) is the pronouncing of a specific speech that is written or preserved by heart.

It has already passed in His saying, exalted is He: (﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl: 98]) in the surah of al-Nahl.

The command to recitation is used in its literal sense of a request to bring about an act in the present or the future. So what is requested by His saying "Read" is that he perform the recitation in the present or in the near future, i.e., that he say what will be dictated to him. The indication that it is a command to recite in the near future is that no speech had previously been dictated to him that was memorised so that he would be asked to recite it, nor had a written sheet been handed to him so that he would be asked to read it. He is like a teacher who says to a student: "Write," so the student prepares to write what he will be dictated.

In the hadith of the two Sahihs, from 'Aisha - may Allah be pleased with her - her words in it: "Until the Truth came to him while he was in the Cave of Hira. The angel came to him and said: 'Read.' He said: I said: 'I am not a reader.' Then he seized me and pressed me until I reached the limit of exhaustion, then he released me and said: 'Read.' I said: 'I am not a reader.' Then he seized me and pressed me a second time until I reached the limit of exhaustion, then he released me and said: 'Read,' and I said: 'I am not a reader.' Then he seized me and pressed me a third time until I reached the limit of exhaustion, then he released me and said: (﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾) to (﴿what he did not know﴾ [al-'Alaq: 5])."

This hadith was related by 'Aisha from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), by her saying: "He said: 'I said: I am not a reader.'" All that she mentioned in it, which she related from him, is undoubtedly so. She also said in it: "So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned with them, his heart trembling," meaning he returned with the verses that had been dictated to him, i.e., he returned clothed with them, i.e., with their comprehension.

This indicates that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) received what was revealed to him and recited it at that time. What makes this clearer is her words in the hadith: "Khadijah took him to Waraqah ibn Nawfal, and Khadijah said to him: 'O cousin, listen to your nephew.'" Meaning: listen to the word that was revealed to him. This indicates that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when it was said to him after the third squeezing (ghatta) (﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾), the five verses, had recited them at that very moment as Allah commanded him, and returned from the Cave of Hira to his house reciting them. In this view, the angel's saying "Read" to him on the three occasions is a repetition of the word sent down from Allah, a repeated re-articulation to make him familiar with recitation, which he had not learned before.

The verb "Read" (iqra') has no object mentioned, either because it is treated as intransitive, meaning the intention is simply to bring about recitation, or because the thing read is evident from the context, and its estimated object is: "Read what We will convey to you of the Qur'an."

His saying: "in the name of your Lord" (bismi rabbika) has several interpretations.

The first: that it is the beginning of a speech after the phrase "Read," and it is the first of what is read, i.e., say: "In the name of Allah," so the bā' is for seeking help (isti'anah), and it may be connected to an omitted verb estimated as "begin." It may also be connected to the second "Read," and its placement before its complement is for emphasis on the matter of the name of Allah. The meaning of seeking help by the name of Allah is mentioning His name at this recitation; and the insertion of the word "name" (ism) is because seeking help is by mentioning His name, exalted is He, not by His essence, as has passed in the discussion of the basmalah. This interpretation requires that the Prophet (ﷺ) said "In the name of Allah" when he received this sentence.

The second: that the bā' is for accompaniment (musahabah), and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the second "Read," placed before its governing verb for restriction (ikhtisas), i.e., read what will be revealed to you accompanied by your recitation of the name of your Lord. The accompaniment is that of understanding and attentiveness to His majesty. This constitutes an affirmation of Allah's oneness in divinity and a nullification of calling upon the names of idols, which the polytheists used to do, saying: "In the name of al-Lat, in the name of al-'Uzza," as has passed in the basmalah. Thus this is the first of the principles of Islam to come, and with it the first of the revelation was opened.

The third: that the bā' carries the meaning of 'alā (upon), as in His saying, exalted is He: (﴿Of whom, if you entrust him with a qintar﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]), i.e., upon a qintar. The meaning is: read upon the name of your Lord, i.e., upon His permission, i.e., the angel came to you upon the name of your Lord, i.e., sent from your Lord. Thus the mention of "name" in this reading is necessary.

صفحة ٤٣٧
The proper name Allah has been replaced by the attribute "your Lord" (rabbika), because the attribute of Lord indicates compassion toward the one nurtured and care for him, together with what results from mentioning it, namely its being attached to the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ), an attachment indicating that He alone is his Lord, as a refutation of those who made for themselves lords besides Allah. Thus this verse became a foundation of tawhid in Islam.
The attribute of the Lord is expressed through the relative clause (﴿who created﴾), because in that there is an argument for Allah's singularity in divinity, since this Qur'an would be recited to the polytheists, as the relative form implies the cause of the predicate. If the cause of directing attention to the mention of the Lord's name is that He is the Creator, this indicates the invalidity of directing attention to the mention of others who do not create. The polytheists used to direct attention to the name of al-Lat and the name of al-'Uzza, yet they acknowledged that Allah is the Creator, as He said: (﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: Allah﴾ [Luqman: 25]). Since the setting was the beginning of Islam, the religion of tawhid, it required mentioning the most indicative attributes of His oneness.

The clause (﴿created man from a clot﴾) may be an apposition (badal) to the clause (﴿who created﴾), an apposition of detail from a general statement, if no object is estimated for it, or an apposition of part if a general object is estimated for it. The route of apposition was chosen because of the generality it contains at the outset, to establish the argument that all created things are in need of Him, exalted is He, since the setting was the beginning of establishing the religion of Islam. Thus in the general statement there is a presentation of the proof with brevity, together with what it conveys of generality; then the detail follows to reinforce the establishment of the proof.

It may also be an explanation (bayan) of (﴿who created﴾) if an object is estimated for the first verb "created," an object indicated by its explanation, so the sense of the sentence would be: Read in the name of your Lord who created man from a clot.

The absence of a mentioned object for "created" may be because the verb is treated as intransitive, i.e., the one who is the Creator; or because the object is omitted to intend generality, i.e., He created all created things; or because its estimate is "who created man," relying on what follows in His saying "created man." These are the meanings in the verse.

صفحة ٤٣٨
The creation of man was singled out for mention among the rest of created things, because it is the most constant in the setting of argument, since no one among people is unaware of himself, and it is inevitable that the thought of seeking the One who created and brought him into being should occur to him. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: (﴿And in yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21]).
In it there is also an allusion to the foolishness of the polytheists who went astray from the tawhid of Allah, exalted is He, although the proof of oneness exists within themselves.

In His saying: (﴿from a clot﴾) there is an indication of the wondrous stages and attributes contained in the origin of man's creation, which made him the sovereign of this terrestrial world.

The clot (‘alaq) is a collective noun whose singular is 'alaqah, a piece the size of a finger-joint of thick coagulated blood, still moist and not yet dried. It was named thus by comparison to a small worm called 'alaqah, which is dark red and found in fresh waters; it sucks blood from animals when its proboscis clings to their skin, and it may enter the mouth of a beast, especially horses and mules, and cling to its palate without the animal noticing it.

The meaning of (﴿created man from a clot﴾) is that the sperm of the male and the ovum of the female, after mixing and the passing of a sufficient period, become a clot; when they become a clot they have entered the stages of formation. The clot was made the origin of creation, and the drop (nutfah) was not made the origin of creation, because nutfah is well known as the water of the man; were it not mixed with the female's ovum, the clot would not come to be and the embryo would not form. In this there is an indication that the creation of man from a clot, then his progress to the full maturity of his strength, is a creation that contains latent powers and great capacities, the furthest of which is the capacity for knowledge and writing.

Among the scientific miracles of the Qur'an is the mention of the clot, because what is established in science now is that man is formed from a very small ovum, invisible except through a magnifying lens by many times, which at the beginning of its appearance is spherical in shape, floating in the menstrual blood of the woman. It does not accept formation until the man's sperm mixes with it and blends with it, and then it begins to form if no obstacle hinders it, as He, exalted is He, said: (﴿formed and unformed﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]). When it begins to form and grow, its roundness lengthens slightly, so it resembles the clot that is in water with complete resemblance in the fineness of its body, its colour matching the colour of the blood in which it floats, and in its floating in a liquid as the clot floats. This has been mentioned in the surah of Ghafir, and I pointed to it in the tenth introduction.

صفحة ٤٣٩
The meaning of the particle (min) is beginning (ibtida').
The second verb "Read" is an emphasis of the first "Read," for the sake of stressing this matter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 96, verses 3–5:

﴿And your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ ﴿Who taught by the pen﴾ ﴿taught man what he did not know﴾.

This is a sentence conjoined to the sentence "﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾" [al-'Alaq: 1], so it has the status of a fresh statement (isti'naf). "Your Lord" (rabbuka) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is either "﴿Who taught by the pen﴾" or the sentence "﴿taught man what he did not know﴾". This fresh statement is explanatory (bayani).

If you consider the verse on its own, apart from what the report of 'A'isha contains concerning the occasion of its revelation, the fresh statement arises from a question that stirs in the mind of the Messenger (ﷺ): how am I to read when I do not know how to read or write? The answer is that the One who taught reading by means of the pen, that is, by means of writing, will teach you what you did not know.

If you combine the verse with the aforementioned hadith, the fresh statement is a reply to his saying to Jibril: "I am not one who reads" (ma ana bi-qari'). The meaning is: there is no wonder in your being able to read even though you were not previously knowledgeable in reading, since knowledge of reading is acquired by other means, such as dictation, instruction and inspiration. God taught Adam the names, and Adam was not a reader.

The apparent form would have been "and taught by the pen", but the noun is used in place of a pronoun to emphasise what "your Lord" implies of the care stated in "﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾" [al-'Alaq: 1], and that this reading is one of the affairs of the Lord, which He singled out for His servant, completing the blessing of lordship (ni'mat al-rububiyyah) upon him.

Also, so that the description "﴿the Most Generous﴾" follows the wording of "Lord".

The description "﴿the Most Generous﴾" (al-Akram) is formed to indicate the strength of the attribute of generosity, and it is not formed for comparison (al-mufadalah); rather, the comparative sense is negated from it.

Generosity (al-karam) is bestowing a gift of what benefits the recipient, and the blessings of God are great and countless, beginning with the blessing of bringing into existence, and the manner of creation and sustenance.

These five verses at the beginning of the surah have gathered the foundations of the divine attributes: the description of the Lord includes existence and oneness; the description "﴿Who created﴾" [al-'Alaq: 1] and the description "﴿Who taught by the pen﴾" entail attributes of action, along with the close inference they contain to the establishment of the attributes indicated, by what the relative construction (mawsuliyyah) implies of an indication to the reason for the construction of the predicate mentioned with it. The description "﴿the Most Generous﴾" includes attributes of perfection and exemption from deficiencies.

The two objects of "﴿taught by the pen﴾" are omitted, indicated by His saying "﴿by the pen﴾". Its estimate is: He taught the scribes, or He taught people writing. The Arabs used to exalt the knowledge of writing and regarded it as one of the distinctive features of the People of the Book, as Abu Hayyah al-Numayri said:

"As the book was inscribed by the hand of a Jewish man one day, approaching or removing [letters]."

Whoever knows writing boasts of his knowledge, and the poet said:

"I learned the abjad and the alphabet of Murámir, ∗∗∗ and I blackened my garments, though I am not a scribe."

It is mentioned that the appearance of script among the Arabs first occurred among the people of al-Anbar. Harb ibn Umayyah brought writing to the Hijaz, having learned it from Aslam ibn Sidrah, and Aslam had learned it from Murámir ibn Murrah. Script had earlier been known among Himyar in Yemen, and it is called al-Musnad.

The singling out of this relative clause for mention, and making it an interjection between the subject and the predicate, serves to indicate the removal of what occurred to the mind of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the impossibility of reading for him, since he does not know writing, so how could reading be possible? When he said to the angel "«I am not one who reads»" three times, because his saying "«I am not one who reads»" was an excuse for being unable to comply with his command "Read" (iqra'). The meaning is that He who taught people writing by the pen and reading is able to teach you reading while you do not know writing.

The pen (al-qalam): a splinter of reed that is thinned and shaped, and planed with a knife so that it is smooth between the fingers, and its tip is split lengthwise for about half a finger-joint. When that tip is wetted with liquid ink, it is used to write on paper or the like. It was previously discussed at His saying: "﴿When they cast their pens, which of them should take charge of Mary﴾" [Al 'Imran: 44], in the surah of Al 'Imran.

The sentence "﴿taught man what he did not know﴾" is the predicate of "﴿And your Lord is the Most Generous﴾", and what lies between them is an interjection.

The definiteness of "al-insan" (man) may be the definiteness of the genus, in which case it is an ascent in informing of what God has decreed concerning the teaching of man, by generalising the teaching after specifying teaching by the pen.

From the mention of teaching by the pen and the more general teaching there arises an indication of what man receives of teachings, whether by lesson or by reading books, and that the acquisition of knowledge depends on three matters:

The first: taking from others through discussion and reading, and the means to these are writing and reading books, for by writing it became possible for nations to record the opinions of human scholars and transmit them to distant regions and to coming generations.

The second: receiving from mouths through lessons and dictation.

The third: what minds spark forth of inferences and inventions. These two are included under His saying "﴿taught man what he did not know﴾".

In this there is reassurance for the soul of the Prophet (ﷺ) that his not knowing writing does not prevent his reading, for God taught man what he did not know. So He who taught reading to people who know writing is able to teach you reading without prior knowledge of writing.

His saying "﴿what he did not know﴾" indicates that knowledge is preceded by ignorance, so every knowledge acquired is knowledge of what was not previously known. That is: do not let it dishearten you from becoming knowledgeable in the Qur'an and the Sharia that you do not know how to read what is written by the pen. The verse also indicates attention to the knowledge of writing, and that God willed that what was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) of the Qur'an be written down; for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) appointed scribes for the revelation from the beginning of his mission.

In limiting the command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to "read" and then informing him that God taught man by the pen, there is an indication of the continuation of the attribute of being unlettered (ummiyyah) for the Prophet (ﷺ), since it is a complementary attribute for the inimitability of the Qur'an. He, the Exalted, said: "﴿And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand; otherwise the falsifiers would have had cause for doubt﴾" [al-'Ankabut: 48].

These are the last of the five verses which were the first to be revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the cave of Hira'.

﴿And your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ ﴿Who taught by the pen﴾ ﴿taught man what he did not know﴾.

This is a sentence conjoined to the sentence "﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾" [al-'Alaq: 1], so it has the status of a fresh statement (isti'naf). "Your Lord" (rabbuka) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is either "﴿Who taught by the pen﴾" or the sentence "﴿taught man what he did not know﴾". This fresh statement is explanatory (bayani).

If you consider the verse on its own, apart from what the report of 'A'isha contains concerning the occasion of its revelation, the fresh statement arises from a question that stirs in the mind of the Messenger (ﷺ): how am I to read when I do not know how to read or write? The answer is that the One who taught reading by means of the pen, that is, by means of writing, will teach you what you did not know.

If you combine the verse with the aforementioned hadith, the fresh statement is a reply to his saying to Jibril: "I am not one who reads" (ma ana bi-qari'). The meaning is: there is no wonder in your being able to read even though you were not previously knowledgeable in reading, since knowledge of reading is acquired by other means, such as dictation, instruction and inspiration. God taught Adam the names, and Adam was not a reader.

The apparent form would have been "and taught by the pen", but the noun is used in place of a pronoun to emphasise what "your Lord" implies of the care stated in "﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾" [al-'Alaq: 1], and that this reading is one of the affairs of the Lord, which He singled out for His servant, completing the blessing of lordship (ni'mat al-rububiyyah) upon him.

Also, so that the description "﴿the Most Generous﴾" follows the wording of "Lord".

The description "﴿the Most Generous﴾" (al-Akram) is formed to indicate the strength of the attribute of generosity, and it is not formed for comparison (al-mufadalah); rather, the comparative sense is negated from it.

Generosity (al-karam) is bestowing a gift of what benefits the recipient, and the blessings of God are great and countless, beginning with the blessing of bringing into existence, and the manner of creation and sustenance.

These five verses at the beginning of the surah have gathered the foundations of the divine attributes: the description of the Lord includes existence and oneness; the description "﴿Who created﴾" [al-'Alaq: 1] and the description "﴿Who taught by the pen﴾" entail attributes of action, along with the close inference they contain to the establishment of the attributes indicated, by what the relative construction (mawsuliyyah) implies of an indication to the reason for the construction of the predicate mentioned with it. The description "﴿the Most Generous﴾" includes attributes of perfection and exemption from deficiencies.

The two objects of "﴿taught by the pen﴾" are omitted, indicated by His saying "﴿by the pen﴾". Its estimate is: He taught the scribes, or He taught people writing. The Arabs used to exalt the knowledge of writing and regarded it as one of the distinctive features of the People of the Book, as Abu Hayyah al-Numayri said:

"As the book was inscribed by the hand of a Jewish man one day, approaching or removing [letters]."

Whoever knows writing boasts of his knowledge, and the poet said:

"I learned the abjad and the alphabet of Murámir, ∗∗∗ and I blackened my garments, though I am not a scribe."

It is mentioned that the appearance of script among the Arabs first occurred among the people of al-Anbar. Harb ibn Umayyah brought writing to the Hijaz, having learned it from Aslam ibn Sidrah, and Aslam had learned it from Murámir ibn Murrah. Script had earlier been known among Himyar in Yemen, and it is called al-Musnad.

The singling out of this relative clause for mention, and making it an interjection between the subject and the predicate, serves to indicate the removal of what occurred to the mind of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the impossibility of reading for him, since he does not know writing, so how could reading be possible? When he said to the angel "«I am not one who reads»" three times, because his saying "«I am not one who reads»" was an excuse for being unable to comply with his command "Read" (iqra'). The meaning is that He who taught people writing by the pen and reading is able to teach you reading while you do not know writing.

The pen (al-qalam): a splinter of reed that is thinned and shaped, and planed with a knife so that it is smooth between the fingers, and its tip is split lengthwise for about half a finger-joint. When that tip is wetted with liquid ink, it is used to write on paper or the like. It was previously discussed at His saying: "﴿When they cast their pens, which of them should take charge of Mary﴾" [Al 'Imran: 44], in the surah of Al 'Imran.

The sentence "﴿taught man what he did not know﴾" is the predicate of "﴿And your Lord is the Most Generous﴾", and what lies between them is an interjection.

The definiteness of "al-insan" (man) may be the definiteness of the genus, in which case it is an ascent in informing of what God has decreed concerning the teaching of man, by generalising the teaching after specifying teaching by the pen.

From the mention of teaching by the pen and the more general teaching there arises an indication of what man receives of teachings, whether by lesson or by reading books, and that the acquisition of knowledge depends on three matters:

The first: taking from others through discussion and reading, and the means to these are writing and reading books, for by writing it became possible for nations to record the opinions of human scholars and transmit them to distant regions and to coming generations.

The second: receiving from mouths through lessons and dictation.

The third: what minds spark forth of inferences and inventions. These two are included under His saying "﴿taught man what he did not know﴾".

In this there is reassurance for the soul of the Prophet (ﷺ) that his not knowing writing does not prevent his reading, for God taught man what he did not know. So He who taught reading to people who know writing is able to teach you reading without prior knowledge of writing.

His saying "﴿what he did not know﴾" indicates that knowledge is preceded by ignorance, so every knowledge acquired is knowledge of what was not previously known. That is: do not let it dishearten you from becoming knowledgeable in the Qur'an and the Sharia that you do not know how to read what is written by the pen. The verse also indicates attention to the knowledge of writing, and that God willed that what was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) of the Qur'an be written down; for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) appointed scribes for the revelation from the beginning of his mission.

In limiting the command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to "read" and then informing him that God taught man by the pen, there is an indication of the continuation of the attribute of being unlettered (ummiyyah) for the Prophet (ﷺ), since it is a complementary attribute for the inimitability of the Qur'an. He, the Exalted, said: "﴿And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand; otherwise the falsifiers would have had cause for doubt﴾" [al-'Ankabut: 48].

These are the last of the five verses which were the first to be revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the cave of Hira'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 96, verses 6–10:

﴿Nay! Indeed, man does transgress﴾ ﴿when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾ ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾

This is a fresh beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new resumptive sentence), evident from the fact that it addresses a subject that has no connection to the preceding discourse.

The particle (كَلّا) (kalla) is one of repudiation and refutation. Nothing in the preceding sentence could be the object of such refutation and rebuke. The presence of (كَلّا) at the beginning of the sentence is therefore evidence that what is intended by the rebuke is what is contained in His saying: (﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾), and so on.

It is proper for (كَلّا) to come after a statement, in order to refute it and rebuke its content. Its occurrence here at the beginning of the discourse implies that the meaning of the statement that follows is worthy of refutation and of rebuking the one who says it. So the discourse is begun with the particle of rebuke for the sake of refutation. Of this kind is the opening of a discourse with a negative particle that has nothing after it that could properly follow the particle, as in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"No, by your father, daughter of the 'Amiri, the people will not claim that I flee."*

Muslim narrated from Abu Hazim, from Abu Hurayra, who said: "Abu Jahl said: 'Does Muhammad rub his face in the dust (i.e., prostrate in prayer) among you?' It was said: 'Yes.' He said: 'By al-Lat and al-'Uzza, if I see him doing that, I will surely step on his neck.' Then he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was praying, supposedly intending to step on his neck. But suddenly he was seen retreating on his heels and protecting himself with his hand. It was said to him: 'What is wrong with you, Abu al-Hakam?' He said: 'Between me and him is a trench of fire, a terror, and wings.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'If he had come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb from limb.' He said: 'So Allah revealed, we do not know whether in the hadith of Abu Hurayra or something else that reached him: (﴿Indeed, man does transgress﴾) the verses.'" End of quotation.

[Page 443]

Al-Tabari said: "It has been mentioned that the verse (﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾) and what follows it were revealed concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, because he said, as we have been informed: 'If I see Muhammad praying, I will surely step on his neck.'" Al-Tabari therefore made what was revealed concerning Abu Jahl begin with His saying: (﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾).

The way to reconcile the two reports is this: part of what was revealed concerning Abu Jahl is the intended matter, namely that which begins with (﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾), etc., and part of it is a preparation and introduction, namely (﴿Indeed, man does transgress﴾) up to (﴿the return﴾).

The scholars differed as to whether these verses up to the end of the surah were revealed immediately after the five preceding verses. They considered it one of the things that conflicts with this that the mention of prayer appears in them, and what is narrated concerning the occasion of their revelation of Abu Jahl's statement, based on the premise that prayer was prescribed on the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey), which occurred several years after the beginning of prophethood. Some said: these verses were revealed after the first five verses of this surah, and other Qur'an was revealed between them, and then these verses were revealed, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded that they be joined to them. Others said: this surah was not the first thing revealed of the Qur'an.

I do not see a conflict that leads to such confusion. What is deduced from the various reports about the beginning of revelation and the events that followed it is that revelation paused after the revelation of the first five verses of this surah, during that first interval which we mentioned at the beginning of the surah of al-Duha. There is another pause in revelation which Ibn Ishaq mentioned after he mentioned the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an, and this indicates that it occurred immediately after the revelation of the first five verses. However, their opinions differed concerning the duration of the pause. Al-Suhayli said: the duration was two years, and this is far-fetched. Determining its duration is not an important matter; what is important is that we are certain that the Prophet ﷺ, during the period of the pause in revelation, would see Jibril and receive revelation from him which was not from the Qur'an.

Al-Suhayli said in al-Rawd al-Unf: al-Harbi mentioned that the prayer before the Isra' was a prayer before the sunset (i.e., the 'Asr) and a prayer before its rising (i.e., the Subh). Yahya ibn Sallam said the same, and said: the Isra' and the prescription of the five prayers occurred a year before the Hijra. End of quotation. So the correct view is that the prayer which the Prophet ﷺ used to perform was other than the five prayers; rather, it was an unspecified form of worship without a fixed manner, and it included prostration, based on the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And prostrate and draw near﴾ [al-'Alaq: 19], which he performed in the Masjid al-Haram or elsewhere in the sight of the polytheists, and this greatly angered Abu Jahl, so he forbade him from it.

[Page 444]

The correct view is that these verses up to the rest of the surah were revealed after a short interval from the revelation of the beginning of the surah, during which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed and the news of the beginning of revelation and the descent of the Qur'an spread. This is in accordance with the principle that consecutive verses in recitation are generally consecutive in revelation, except where a clear proof establishes that a later part was revealed later. It is also in accordance with the sound view, which should not be turned away from, that this surah is the first surah revealed.

The position of His saying (﴿Indeed, man does transgress﴾ ﴿when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾) is that of an introduction to what follows it, namely His saying (﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾) up to His saying (﴿do not obey him﴾) [al-'Alaq: 19], because its content is a comprehensive statement including the content of (﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾) up to His saying (﴿let him call his council﴾) [al-'Alaq: 17].

The meaning is: what Abu Jahl said arises from his transgression due to his wealth, as is the nature of man.

The definite article in (al-insan, "man") is generic, i.e., it is part of human nature that man transgresses when he perceives self-sufficiency in himself. The lam (لام) implies customary comprehensiveness, i.e., most people at that time, except those whom their character or religion protects.

Emphasizing the statement with the particle of emphasis and the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') is for the purpose of increasing its certainty, because of its strangeness, to the point that it is as though it is something the listener might be expected to doubt.

Al-tughyan (الطُّغْيان, transgression) means arrogance and pride.

Al-istighna' (الِاسْتِغْناء, self-sufficiency) means intense wealth. The sin and ta' in it are for intensification in the occurrence of the act, like istajaba (he responded) and istaqarra (he settled).

The phrase (أنْ راءَهُ, "that he sees him") is connected to (يَطْغى, "transgresses") with the lam of causation deleted, because the deletion of the preposition is common and widespread. The implied meaning is: Indeed, man transgresses because of his seeing himself as self-sufficient.

The cause of this disposition is that self-sufficiency gives its possessor the notion that he does not need anyone else, and that others are in need, so he sees himself as greater than those in need. This illusion continues to grow in his soul until it becomes a character trait, where no restraint holds him back from religion or sound reasoning. So he oppresses people, feeling that he does not fear their force, because he has what he uses to repel aggression: an array of weapons, servants, helpers, those who depend on him, and those who benefit from his wealth, such as partners, workers and hired laborers. Thus he is in a state of might in his own estimation.

This verse has clarified a great psychological and ethical truth and has warned against allowing it to penetrate the soul.

In the speech of the Arabs, two pronouns referring to the same antecedent cannot be combined, one as subject and the other as object, unless the governing verb is of the class of (ظَنَّ, "to think") and its sisters, as in this verse. Of this is His saying, the Exalted: (﴿He said: "Have you seen this one whom you have honored over me?"﴾) [al-Isra': 62] in the surah of al-Isra'. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs drop the self-pronoun from this category (i.e., the category of verbs of thinking and supposing). They say: ra'aytuni (I saw myself) and hasibtuni (I reckoned myself), and mata turaka kharijan (when do you see yourself going out), and mata tazunnuka kharijan (when do you think you are going out). Many grammarians consider the visual (بَصَرِيَّة) verb ra'a (رَأى, "to see") to be joined to the mental (قَلْبِيَّة) ra'a, as in the verse of Qutari ibn al-Fuja'a:

*"Indeed, I see myself a target for the spears, sometimes from my right and sometimes in front of me."*

Rare is the verse of al-Namir ibn Tawlab:

*"I have spent the night guarding myself alone, and the cry of the beasts prevents me, they howl and the owl (screams)."*

All of them recited (أنْ رَآهُ, "that he sees him") with an alif after the hamza. Ibn Mujahid narrated from Qunbul that he recited it from Ibn Kathir as (رَأْهُ, "ra'hu") without the alif after the hamza. Ibn Mujahid said: this is an error. This statement of Ibn Mujahid is not to be heeded after he asserted that he narrated it from Qunbul; but this was not narrated by anyone other than Ibn Mujahid from Qunbul, so it is an unusual reading from Qunbul.

I also add to these verbs the verbs (فَقَدَ, "to lose") and (عَدِمَ, "to lack"), when they are used in supplication, such as the saying of one who says: faqadtuni (may I be lost) and 'adimtuni (may I be lacking).

[Page 446]

The clause (﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾) is parenthetical between the introduction and the main purpose, and the address is to the Prophet ﷺ. The meaning is: the return of the transgressor is to Allah. This is an exhortation and a threat by way of allusion to those tyrants who hear it, and an instruction and confirmation for the Prophet ﷺ, i.e., do not let the transgression of the transgressor grieve you, for his return is to Me. The return of the transgressor is to punishment. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Indeed, Hell has been an ambush﴾) [al-Naba': 21] (﴿for the transgressors, a place of return﴾) [al-Naba': 22]. It is also an exhortation to the transgressor that his wealth does not repel death from him. Death is a return to Allah, as in His saying: (﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet it﴾) [al-Inshiqaq: 6].

There is another meaning in it: his self-sufficiency is not real, because he is in need of Allah in his most important affairs, and he does not know what his Lord will bring him to in consequences. So his false wealth in this life should not make him more; thus the return (al-ruj'a) is used in its figurative sense, which is the need for the one to whom one returns. The emphasis of the statement with (إنّ, "indeed") takes into account the allusive meaning, because most tyrants deny this reality, in that they treat it as if they were deniers of it.

Al-ruj'a (الرُّجْعى, the return), with a damma on the ra', is a verbal noun of (رَجَعَ, "to return") on the pattern fu'la, like al-bushra (good news).

The fronting of (إلى رَبِّكَ, "to your Lord") before (الرُّجْعى, "the return") is for the sake of emphasis on this.

The clause (﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾) up to its end is the intended object of the rebuke conveyed by the particle kalla. This clause is a fresh beginning, a direct resumptive sentence connected to the resumptive sentence beginning with (﴿Indeed, man does transgress﴾).

Regarding (﴿the one who forbids﴾), the scholars agreed that it refers to Abu Jahl, since he said a statement intending to forbid the Prophet ﷺ from praying in the Masjid al-Haram. He said in his assembly: "If I see Muhammad praying at the Ka'ba, I will surely step on his neck." He intended by this statement that it reach the Prophet ﷺ, so it is a threat that implies a prohibition against praying in the Masjid al-Haram. It is not reported that he forbade him directly.

(أرَأيْتَ, "Have you seen") is a word expressing wonder at a situation, said to one who knows that he saw a strange situation. The seeing here is cognitive (علمية); i.e., "Do you know the one who forbids a servant?" and the question concerns that knowledge. The second object of (رَأيْتَ) is elided, indicated by His saying at the end of the verses: (﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾) [al-'Alaq: 14].

[Page 447]

The interrogative is used for wonder, because a strange situation is something about which one asks whether it occurred, as a question of verification and confirmation of its news, since one can hardly believe it. So the use of the interrogative for wonder is a metonymy (majaz mursal) in the structure. The occurrence of the interrogative for wonder is common, as in (﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾) [al-Ghashiyah: 1].

The seeing is cognitive, and the meaning is: what is the most astonishing knowledge that came to you, namely, the one who forbids a servant when he prays. It is also permissible for the seeing to be visual, since it is a narration of an event that occurred in the external world.

The address in (أرَأيْتَ, "Have you seen") is to an unspecified addressee.

By "the servant" is meant the Prophet ﷺ. The use of "servant" here in the sense of one individual among the servants of Allah, i.e., a person, is as in His saying, the Exalted: (﴿We have sent against you servants of Ours of great might﴾) [al-Isra': 5], i.e., men. He turned away from expressing it with a pronoun of address because the wonder is at the very act of forbidding prayer, regardless of the particular identity of the one who prays. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 96, verses 13–14:

﴿Have you seen, if he denies and turns away?﴾ ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾

This is a resumed (mustaʼnafah) sentence serving as a threat and warning against denial and turning away; that is: if he denies what he is called to and turns away, does he suppose that he is unaware that Allah is watching him?

The first object of (raʼayta) is elided, and it is a pronoun referring back to ﴿the one who forbids﴾ [al-ʻAlaq: 9]. The estimated sense is: "Have you seen him, if he denies…" to the end of the verse.

The response (jawab) of ﴿if he denies and turns away﴾ is ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ This is how the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) estimated it, and he did not regard it as obligatory for the response clause to be joined by the fa' (then) when the clause is interrogative. Al-Radi clearly preferred that joining with fa' is not a condition, and he supported this with the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Have you seen, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you suddenly or openly, will any be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?﴾ [al-An'am: 47]. As for the view of the majority of grammarians and al-Zamakhshari in al-Mufassal, it is that joining with fa' is obligatory, and according to their view

صفحة ٤٤٩
the response of the condition must be estimated by what indicates it, ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ The estimate is: "If he denies and turns away, then Allah knows about him," as a metonymy for His threat. The clause ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ is then a resumed sentence denying the ignorance of the denier that Allah will punish him, and the condition and its response serve as the second object.

The statement "Allah sees" is a metonymy for the threat of punishment.

The verb (yaʻlam) is taken to include the meaning of (yuqin, be certain), which is why it takes the preposition bi-.

The verb (raʼayta) here is suspended from acting because of the interrogative in ﴿Does he not know﴾.

The interrogative is a rebuke (inkari), meaning: it was his duty to know this and to protect himself from punishment.

In the words ﴿if he denies and turns away﴾ there is an announcement to the Prophet (ﷺ) that Abu Jahl will deny him when he calls him to Islam and will turn away, and a promise that Allah will take his revenge on him.

The pronoun of ﴿denies and turns away﴾ refers back to ﴿the one who forbids a servant when he prays﴾ [al-ʻAlaq: 9], and the context of the passage returns the pronouns to their differing referents.

The object of (kadhdhaba) is elided because the preceding text indicates it. The estimate is: "if he denies him," that is, the servant who prayed. By this, the three clauses are coherently linked in the attribution of their meanings to "the one who forbids a servant when he prays" and to "the servant who prayed," and doubts that arose in the exegeses are dispelled for you.

The object of (yara) is elided to make it general for every existing thing; and the seeing attributed to Allah the Exalted is the connection of His knowledge to what is perceptible.

Kalla.

He emphasized the first deterrence with the second deterrent particle at the end of the clause, which is its true position, since its counterpart was placed at the beginning of the clause for a purpose that called for suspense.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 96, verse 15–16:

Page 450
﴿Nay, if he does not desist, We will surely seize him by the forelock﴾ ﴿a lying, sinning forelock.﴾

He follows the rebuke with a threat against his act, should he not be restrained and desist from it.

The lam is a preparatory lam (al-lam al-muwatta'ah) introducing the oath; the clause "la-nasfa'an" is the answer to the oath. As for the answer to the condition, it is omitted, its meaning indicated by the answer to the oath.

Al-saf' (سَفْع) means a strong seizing with a pull.

Al-nasiyah (النّاصِيَة) is the front part of the hair of the head. Taking someone by the forelock means taking him in such a way that he has no opportunity to escape; it is a metaphor for seizing him and dragging him to punishment, and it carries humiliation, because they used to grab no one's hair except to strike him or to drag him along. The ba' (باء) that is added to the object, which is attached to the verb, emphasizes the closeness of the grip, and this emphasizes that seizure.

The nun is the light nun of emphasis (nun al-tawkid al-khafifah), which frequently enters an affirmative oath. It is written in the Mushaf as an alif, out of regard for its pronunciation in pause, because the endings of words are most often written with regard to their pronunciation in pause.

The definiteness of "al-nasiyah" is for a presumed known reference (al-'ahd al-taqdiri), i.e., "by his forelock," meaning the forelock of the one who forbids a servant when he prays. This lam is what the grammarians of Kufa call a substitute for the genitive complement (iwad 'an al-mudaf ilayh), and this designation is a good one, though the Basrans rejected it and therefore posited, in such instances, a governing element for the word following the lam.

"Nasiyah" (ناصِيَةٍ) is an apposition (badal) from "al-nasiyah," and its indefiniteness is for the sake of considering the category: meaning, it is of the kind of a lying, sinning forelock.

"Khati'ah" (خاطِئَةٍ) is an active participle from "khati'a" (خَطِئَ) of the pattern "'alima," when one commits a sin (khati'ah), i.e., a wrong. Describing the forelock as lying and sinning is an intellectual metaphor (majaz 'aqli). What is meant is that its owner is lying and its owner is sinning, i.e., guilty. What makes this metaphor pleasing is that it conveys an imagining that lying and error proceed from his forelock, so the forelock deserves to be seized.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 96, verses 17–18:

Page 451
﴿Then let him call his council (nadiyah)﴾ ﴿We shall call the guards of Hell (al-zabaniyah)﴾ ﴿No! [Al-'Alaq: 19].
This is a consequence (tafri') of the promise. The occasion (munasabah) of this is what al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was praying at the Station (al-Maqam), when Abu Jahl passed by him and said: 'O Muhammad, did I not forbid you from this?' and he threatened him. So the Messenger of Allah rebuked him harshly. Abu Jahl said: 'O Muhammad, with what do you threaten me? By Allah, I have more council (nadiyan) than anyone in this valley.' So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Then let him call his council﴾ ﴿We shall call the guards of Hell.﴾" The meaning is that Abu Jahl intended by his words to threaten the Prophet (ﷺ) that he would incite his council against him.

Al-nadi (the council): a name for the place where the people gather. It is said: "The people gathered (nadaw) a gathering (nadwan)" when they assembled. Al-nadwah, with a fatha on the nun, means the group. It is said nadin and nadiyy. This name is not applied to the place except when the people are gathered in it; when they disperse from it, it is no longer a nadi. The term al-nadi is also said of the people's sitting by day; their sitting at night is called al-musamar. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Conversing by night, you talk nonsense﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 67].

Qusayy took for the council of Quraysh a house called Dar al-Nadwah (the House of the Council), near the Sacred Mosque, and made it for their consultations and important affairs. In it marriages were contracted, and in it the young girls were "clothed in armor" (yatadarra'u al-jawari), that is, they were dressed in the shifts (aqmisah), as a public announcement that they had approached the age of puberty. This house was bought by al-Khayzuran, wife of al-Mansur Abu Ja'far, and she included it in the courtyard of the Sacred Mosque. Part of it was added to the Sacred Mosque in the extension of 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, and part in the extension of Abu Ja'far al-Mansur, and the remainder remained as a separate house, in which al-Mahdi stayed in the year 160 during the caliphate of al-Mu'tadid Billah al-'Abbasi. When the Sacred Mosque was extended, the place of Dar al-Nadwah was made a mosque connected to the Sacred Mosque, and it continued so. Then it was demolished and its area was included in the area of the Sacred Mosque in the extension that King Sa'ud ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, king of Hijaz and Najd, added in the year 1379.

The term al-nadi is also applied to those who gather in it, and this is the meaning of Abu Jahl's words: "I have more council (nadiyan) than anyone in this valley," that is, people who sit with me; he means that he is a chief to whom people turn, and this is what is intended here.

Page 452
The application of al-nadi to its people is similar to the application of al-qaryah (the town) to its people in His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], and similar to the application of al-majlis (the assembly) to its people in the words of Dhu al-Rummah:

For them is an assembly, tawny-whiskered, humbled, equal to one another, its free and its slaves alike.

And the application of al-maqamah (the gathering place) to its people in the words of Zuhayr:

Among them are gatherings (maqamat) whose faces are fair, and councils (andiyah) frequented by speech and deed.

That is, people of fair faces who hold gatherings.
And the application of al-majma' (the assembly) to its people in the words of Labid:

Indeed, when the assemblies (majami') meet, there remains among us a mighty warrior whose bodies are large... [the four verses].

The imperative particle (lam al-amr) in ﴿Then let him call﴾ is for incapacitation (lil-ta'jiz), because Abu Jahl threatened the Prophet (ﷺ) with the multitude of his supporters, who are the people of his council. Allah replied to him by commanding him to call his council; for if he called them to assault the Prophet (ﷺ), Allah would call the angels, who would destroy him. This verse is a special miracle (mu'jizah) among the miracles of the Qur'an, for it challenged Abu Jahl with this, and Abu Jahl heard the Qur'an and his supporters heard it, yet none of them dared to assault the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), even though the speech would inflame his zeal.

The attribution of al-nadi to his pronoun (idafat al-nadi ila damirihi) is because he is their chief, and they gather around him. A Bedouin woman said: "Lord of his council, and the protector of his dependents."

His saying ﴿We shall call the guards of Hell﴾ is the answer to the incapacitating command, that is: if he calls his council, we shall call the guards for them. So the verb sanad'u is jussive (majzum) as an answer to the command, and for this reason it is written in the Mushaf without the waw, and without the letter of future (sa-) for emphasis of the verb.

Al-zabaniyah: with a fatha on the zay and a light ya', the plural of zabbani (with a fatha on the zay and a doubled ya'), or the plural of zibniyah (with a kasra on the zay, then a silent ba', then a kasrah on the nun, then a light ya'), or the plural of zibniyy (with a kasra, then a sukun, then a doubled ya'). It is said that it is a collective noun (ism jam') with no singular from its own form, like ababil and 'ababid. This word is derived from al-zabn, which is pushing with force. It is said: "A she-camel that is zabun" when she kicks whoever milks her, and "a war that is zabun" when some of it pushes others through repeated fighting.

Page 453
So al-zabaniyah are those who push people, that is, they push them forcefully. By them is meant the angels of punishment, and al-zabaniyah is also applied to the auxiliaries of the police.

And ﴿No!﴾ [al-'Alaq: 19] is a rebuke to nullify what his saying ﴿Then let him call his council﴾ implied, that is: "and he will not do it." This is an emphasis of the challenge and incapacitation.

And (sanad'u) is written in the Mushaf without a waw after the 'ayn, out of regard for the state of continuity (wasl), for it is neither a place of pause nor a verse-ending.

Part of it was added to the Sacred Mosque in the extension of 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, and part in the extension of Abu Ja'far al-Mansur, and the remainder remained as a separate house, in which al-Mahdi stayed in the year 160 during the caliphate of al-Mu'tadid Billah al-'Abbasi. When the Sacred Mosque was extended, the place of Dar al-Nadwah was made a mosque connected to the Sacred Mosque, and it continued so. Then it was demolished and its area was included in the area of the Sacred Mosque in the extension that King Sa'ud ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, king of Hijaz and Najd, added in the year 1379.

The term al-nadi is also applied to those who gather in it, and this is the meaning of Abu Jahl's words: "I have more council (nadiyan) than anyone in this valley," that is, people who sit with me; he means that he is a chief to whom people turn, and this is what is intended here.

The application of al-nadi to its people is similar to the application of al-qaryah (the town) to its people in His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], and similar to the application of al-majlis (the assembly) to its people in the words of Dhu al-Rummah:

For them is an assembly, tawny-whiskered, humbled, equal to one another, its free and its slaves alike.

And the application of al-maqamah (the gathering place) to its people in the words of Zuhayr:

Among them are gatherings (maqamat) whose faces are fair, and councils (andiyah) frequented by speech and deed.

That is, people of fair faces who hold gatherings.
And the application of al-majma' (the assembly) to its people in the words of Labid:

Indeed, when the assemblies (majami') meet, there remains among us a mighty warrior whose bodies are large... [the four verses].

The imperative particle (lam al-amr) in ﴿Then let him call﴾ is for incapacitation (lil-ta'jiz), because Abu Jahl threatened the Prophet (ﷺ) with the multitude of his supporters, who are the people of his council. Allah replied to him by commanding him to call his council; for if he called them to assault the Prophet (ﷺ), Allah would call the angels, who would destroy him. This verse is a special miracle (mu'jizah) among the miracles of the Qur'an, for it challenged Abu Jahl with this, and Abu Jahl heard the Qur'an and his supporters heard it, yet none of them dared to assault the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), even though the speech would inflame his zeal.

The attribution of al-nadi to his pronoun (idafat al-nadi ila damirihi) is because he is their chief, and they gather around him. A Bedouin woman said: "Lord of his council, and the protector of his dependents."

His saying ﴿We shall call the guards of Hell﴾ is the answer to the incapacitating command, that is: if he calls his council, we shall call the guards for them. So the verb sanad'u is jussive (majzum) as an answer to the command, and for this reason it is written in the Mushaf without the waw, and without the letter of future (sa-) for emphasis of the verb.

Al-zabaniyah: with a fatha on the zay and a light ya', the plural of zabbani (with a fatha on the zay and a doubled ya'), or the plural of zibniyah (with a kasra on the zay, then a silent ba', then a kasrah on the nun, then a light ya'), or the plural of zibniyy (with a kasra, then a sukun, then a doubled ya'). It is said that it is a collective noun (ism jam') with no singular from its own form, like ababil and 'ababid. This word is derived from al-zabn, which is pushing with force. It is said: "A she-camel that is zabun" when she kicks whoever milks her, and "a war that is zabun" when some of it pushes others through repeated fighting.

So al-zabaniyah are those who push people, that is, they push them forcefully. By them is meant the angels of punishment, and al-zabaniyah is also applied to the auxiliaries of the police.

And ﴿No!﴾ [al-'Alaq: 19] is a rebuke to nullify what his saying ﴿Then let him call his council﴾ implied, that is: "and he will not do it." This is an emphasis of the challenge and incapacitation.

And (sanad'u) is written in the Mushaf without a waw after the 'ayn, out of regard for the state of continuity (wasl), for it is neither a place of pause nor a verse-ending.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (*al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*) on Surah 96, verse 19:

﴿Do not obey him, but prostrate and draw near.﴾

This is a summary (*fadhlaka*, a concluding recapitulation) of the preceding discourse, from His words: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ (Al-'Alaq: 9) ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾ (Al-'Alaq: 10). The meaning is: do not abandon your prayer at the Sacred Mosque, and do not fear him.

"Obedience" is used here for the fear that prompts obedience, through figurative usage of the *majaz mursal* type (metonymy, a figure based on a non-analogical relation). The meaning is: do not fear him or be wary of him, for he cannot harm you.

The phrase "Do not obey him" is reinforced by the clause "and prostrate," out of concern for the prayer (*salah*).

He joined "and draw near" to it in order to highlight what prayer contains of God's good pleasure, in that it makes the one who prays draw near to God, the Exalted.

*Iqtirab* (drawing near) is a *ifti'al* form derived from *qurb* (nearness). He expressed it with the *ifti'al* pattern because that pattern carries the sense of effort and seeking, meaning: strive to draw near to God through prayer.

Surah al-Qadr

This surah is named "Surat al-Qadr" (the Surah of Power/Destiny) in the codices of the Qur'an (*masahif*, written copies of the Qur'an), in books of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), and in books of Sunnah (prophetic tradition). Ibn 'Atiyya named it in his tafsir, and Abu Bakr al-Jassas named it in his *Ahkam al-Qur'an* "Surat Laylat al-Qadr" (the Surah of the Night of Power).

It is Meccan according to the majority, and this is the view of Jabir ibn Zayd, and it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak that it is Medinan, and al-Qurtubi attributed this view to most scholars. Al-Waqidi said: it is the first surah revealed in Medina. What favours this is that its evident purpose is to encourage the observance of the Night of Power, and that was only after the obligation of Ramadan following the Hijrah.

Jabir ibn Zayd counted it as the twenty-fifth in the order of the revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat 'Abasa and before Surat al-Shams. As for the view of those who said it is Medinan, it implies that it was revealed after Surat al-Mutaffifin and before Surat al-Baqarah.

Its verses number five according to the Medinan, Basran and Kufan counts, and six according to the Meccan and Syrian counts.
